meters.label: Places to write a new rule

frames.narration: An Order has four rules: ship only when paid, ship only when not empty, add nothing after shipping, discount at most 50%. Five code paths each try all four forbidden changes: 20 attempts.
Anemic: the Order is only fields, and the rules sit in OrderService. The checkout, the REST controller and the nightly job call the service, and all 12 of their forbidden attempts are refused.

The support admin tool and the CSV import write the fields directly. Nothing checks them: all 4 forbidden changes get in through each of them, 8 of the 20 attempts. The rules were never wrong, only optional.

A new rule arrives: no discount on a shipped order. In the anemic design it is written in the service and again in each of the 2 paths that bypass it: 3 places, and the next developer has to know about all of them.

Rich: the fields are private and the Order's own methods hold the rules. All 5 paths go through ship, addItem and applyDiscount, because there is no other way in: 0 of 20 forbidden changes get in, and the new rule is written in 1 place.

Rich everywhere: the Order also gets save(), emailReceipt() and renderInvoice(). It still blocks all 20 attempts, but testing one rule now needs a database and a mailer, and a plain Country table gets 8 methods where 2 were enough.
Put behaviour where there are rules to keep, and keep persistence and messaging outside. For simple CRUD, with nothing to protect, plain data is fine.
